You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
The feature launched on a Tuesday. By Friday, I was checking the analytics dashboard like refreshing it might change the result.

Almost nobody had used it.

We had spent six weeks building it. The design was thoughtful. The engineering was solid. The launch announcement got a few enthusiastic replies.

And then, nothing.

My first instinct was to blame discoverability. Maybe the button was in the wrong place. Maybe we needed another email. Maybe users just needed time.

Those were easier explanations than the one we eventually found.

We had taken a handful of feature requests as proof of demand without asking enough questions about the work behind them.

People had asked for a better way to generate reports. We built a flexible reporting tool with filters, saved views, and export options.

When we went back and watched them work, most didn’t want to build a report at all. They wanted to answer one recurring question before a weekly meeting. Their spreadsheet already did that, badly but predictably.

Our feature gave them more options. It also gave them another thing to learn and maintain.

The uncomfortable part was that we could have learned this before writing much code. We had asked, “Would this be useful?” We hadn’t asked, “Show me what you did last Friday.”

That changed how I approach feature requests.

Now I want to see the current workaround. I want to know how often the problem happens, what it costs, and what someone would have to give up to use our solution.

I also try to agree on what meaningful usage would look like before we start building. It makes the conversation after launch more honest, even when the numbers are disappointing.

We eventually replaced most of that reporting tool with a simple weekly summary. Fewer settings, less flexibility, much more use.

I still wish we had those six weeks back. But I’m glad we stopped trying to improve the button and started asking why nobody needed to click it.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Two years ago I spent about six weeks building a feature that, as far as I can tell, was used by eleven people. I am not rounding.

It was a scheduling tool inside a reporting product. Customers could set up a report to generate itself every Monday and land in their inbox. We had heard the request in at least a dozen customer calls. I had a spreadsheet of quotes. When we shipped it, the announcement email got a decent open rate and a few replies saying "finally." Then nothing. Usage flatlined within a month and never recovered.

For a while I told myself the problem was discoverability. We moved the button. We added a tooltip. We mentioned it in onboarding. Still nothing. Eventually I did the thing I should have done first, which was call the people who had asked for it and ask why they weren't using it.

The answer was boring and kind of humbling. Most of them already had a workaround. They had a calendar reminder, or an assistant who pulled the report, or a habit of checking on Monday mornings with their coffee. The workaround was slightly annoying, which is why they mentioned it when we asked what was annoying. But it was not annoying enough to change a routine they had already built. The request was real. The pain was real. The pain just wasn't big enough to justify learning something new, even something small.

I had been treating a complaint as a commitment. Those are very different things. People will happily tell you what bothers them. They are much less likely to tell you, or even know, what they would actually change their behavior for. And I had never asked the follow up question that matters, which is some version of "what are you doing about this today?" If the answer is "nothing, I just live with it," that's a signal the pain is tolerable, and tolerable pain rarely gets a feature adopted.

The other thing I learned is that the sunk cost after shipping is worse than the sunk cost before. Once the feature existed, we kept spending small amounts of time on it. Fixing an edge case here, answering a support ticket there, making sure a redesign didn't break it. It sat in the codebase like a houseguest nobody invited but nobody wanted to be rude to. We finally removed it last spring. Nobody wrote in.

I still ask customers what frustrates them. I just don't stop there anymore. I ask what they've tried, how often it actually comes up, and what they'd give up to have it fixed. Most of the time the honest answer is "not much," and I've learned to take that as useful information rather than a challenge.

The feature didn't fail because we built it badly. It failed because we confused being asked for something with being needed. That distinction has probably saved me more time than anything I've shipped since.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

three-item list: filters, saved views, and export options
tells_B: negative parallelism: didn't fail because / failed because
triad of short uniform sentences: moved button / added tooltip / mentioned in onboarding
triad list: calendar reminder, assistant, habit
question followed by its own answer: what are you doing...? If the answer is...
